title: IB Enquiry Upon Results: Is a Remark Worth It?
summary: IB enquiry upon results explained for students and parents. Assess boundaries, risks and university stakes before deciding whether to request a remark.
body_markdown:
Results day can turn two years of work into a row of numbers. One subject catches your eye. The grade is lower than expected, perhaps by only a mark or two, and a difficult question follows: should you challenge it?


An **IB enquiry upon results** can be worth it when your scaled mark is close to the next grade boundary, the subject involves judgement-based marking, and a higher grade would materially affect your diploma, university place or another important outcome. It is usually less compelling when you are several marks below the boundary or when nothing meaningful would change.


There is also a real risk. The International Baccalaureate states that a re-mark can move a subject grade **up or down** , so the decision should be made from the numbers rather than disappointment alone. Your coordinator must submit the request on your behalf, and written consent is required because the grade could fall.


### The short decision checklist


Before requesting a re-mark, ask your IB coordinator for the information needed to answer five questions:


- How many scaled marks separate you from the next boundary?
- Could your current grade fall if marks are removed?
- Which components are eligible for re-marking?
- Would a higher subject grade change your diploma total or university position?
- What fee, deadline and expected processing time apply to your session?


The first question is the natural starting point. RevisionDojo's[IB Grade Calculator](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib-grade-calculator) helps you check exact conversions in the Grade boundaries tool rather than relying on a vague feeling that you were "close."


A student asks to zoom out while a parent magnifies the question mark on a results sheet


### What an IB enquiry upon results actually does


Students often call the process a remark, but the formal name is an Enquiry Upon Results, commonly shortened to EUR. The[IB's guidance on getting results](https://www.ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/assessment-and-exams/getting-results/) explains that schools place EUR requests for students after results are issued.


The re-mark service is generally known as a Category 1 enquiry. According to the IB's[assessment FAQ](https://www.ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/assessment-and-exams/getting-results/assessment-faq/) , the relevant externally assessed work is marked again by a senior examiner. It is not a negotiation, an opportunity to submit extra evidence or a general reconsideration of how hard you worked.


Other EUR services may serve different purposes, such as returning assessment material or asking for feedback on a group of candidates. That distinction matters. A family seeking an individual grade change should confirm the exact service with the school's DP coordinator rather than assuming that every enquiry produces a fresh individual mark.


### Follow the marks, not the surprise


Imagine a clearly dated illustration. In July 2026, a hypothetical student named Maya opens her results and sees a 5 in English A. She expected a 6. Her first instinct is that the grade must be wrong.


Expectation is emotionally important, but it is not enough to assess a re-mark. Maya needs her scaled total and the session-specific **IB grade boundaries** . If she is one mark below a 6, a modest upward change could alter her grade. If she is seven marks below it, the same request requires a much larger movement.


A useful calculation is:


Distance to next grade=next boundary−current scaled mark\\text{Distance to next grade} = \\text{next boundary} - \\text{current scaled mark}

Suppose Maya's scaled mark is 59 and the illustrative boundary for a 6 is 60. Her distance is one mark. These figures are an example only, not an actual boundary for any subject, level or session. Real boundaries vary, so use the official information supplied through your school and verify the conversion with RevisionDojo's Grade boundaries tool.


This is where calm replaces guesswork. The question is no longer, "Do I deserve a 6?" It becomes, "Is a movement of at least one scaled mark plausible and valuable enough to accept the downside?"


### When a remark is more likely to be worth it


A request deserves serious consideration when several factors align.


### You are very close to the upper boundary


Proximity does not guarantee success, but it reduces the size of the required mark movement. Being one mark short is fundamentally different from being six marks short.


Do not confuse a component mark with the final scaled subject mark. Components can have different weightings, and scaling may affect how a raw change contributes to the subject total. Ask your coordinator to explain the figure you are comparing.


### The assessment involves examiner judgement


Essays, extended responses and interpretation can involve professional judgement within a mark scheme. A second senior examiner may reach a slightly different result. More objective responses leave less room for legitimate variation, although administrative or marking errors are still possible.


This is not a reason to assume an essay will gain marks. It simply affects the plausibility of movement and should be considered alongside the boundary distance.


### One grade has a meaningful consequence


A re-mark becomes more rational when an increase would meet a university condition, secure the diploma, satisfy an HL requirement or change a total relevant to admission. Contact the university promptly if your offer is at stake. Ask whether it will hold your place while an enquiry is processed and what evidence it needs from your school.


Keep the university informed rather than waiting silently. Timing rules and institutional policies differ, and neither the IB nor RevisionDojo can promise how a university will respond.


### When caution is wiser


A re-mark is usually harder to justify when the required movement is large, the grade has no practical consequence, or your current mark is also close to the lower boundary.


That final point is easy to miss. Because **IB grades** may rise or fall after re-marking, the useful picture has two distances:


Question Why it matters


How far am I from the next grade? Shows the minimum upward movement needed


How far am I from the lower grade? Reveals the potential grade-level downside


What changes if I gain a grade? Tests whether the benefit is meaningful


What changes if I lose a grade? Makes the risk concrete


The fee matters too, especially if multiple subjects are being considered. Schools may also have internal administrative dates earlier than the IB's final deadline. Confirm current costs, refund conditions and dates directly with your coordinator because they can vary by session and school arrangements.


### Build the decision around evidence


Maya's next move should not be to replay every difficult exam question. Memory becomes less reliable under stress, and feeling confident after an exam does not reveal how the response matched the mark scheme.


Instead, she can use a simple sequence:


1. Obtain the component and scaled marks available through the school.
2. Check the correct subject, level and examination-session boundaries.
3. Calculate the distances to both adjacent grade boundaries.
4. Identify the concrete effect of an increase or decrease.
5. Discuss eligible components, fees and deadlines with the coordinator.
6. Contact the university immediately if an offer could be affected.
7. Give written consent only after understanding that the result can fall.


The IB's published[Diploma Programme regulations](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/become-an-ib-school/pdfs/dp-2026-general-regulations.pdf) confirm that enquiries must be submitted by the school and that re-marking may produce a higher or lower subject grade. That makes the coordinator more than an administrator. They are the bridge between your analysis and the formal process.


### What to do after making the decision


If you request the enquiry, keep copies of relevant messages and continue meeting university instructions. Do not treat a possible increase as confirmed until the revised result is formally issued.


If you decide against it, that does not mean you have accepted that the original expectation was foolish. It means the expected benefit did not justify the cost and risk. Good decisions are judged by the information available when they are made, not only by the outcome we wish had occurred.


Then turn toward the next step. RevisionDojo's Questionbank, Study Notes, Flashcards and AI Chat can help diagnose knowledge gaps if you plan to retake. Grading tools can make written practice more deliberate, while Predicted Papers and Mock Exams build timed familiarity. The Coursework Library and Tutors add support when independent revision is not enough.


The first step, however, is smaller. Find the right boundary and measure the gap. Use RevisionDojo's Grade boundaries tool for **exact conversions** , then take those figures to your coordinator. A result may feel like a verdict. Properly understood, it is first a set of numbers, and numbers give you somewhere sensible to begin.
